1.pericope_label: Eve bare Cain, and said, I have gotten a man from the LORD

schools.summary: Gill treats the opening verb as a modest expression and reports the rabbinic view that Adam had known his wife before he sinned, objecting that children begotten in innocence would have been free from the corruption afterwards contracted, and preferring the opinion that some considerable time passed. Calvin makes the same point doctrinally: the benediction to increase and multiply was not abolished by sin, and Adam's heart was divinely confirmed so that he did not shrink from the production of offspring; yet as he recognised at the very commencement the truly paternal moderation of God's anger, so he was afterwards compelled to taste the bitter fruits of his own sin when Cain slew Abel. On Eve's exclamation Calvin lists three renderings which all tend to the same point, that she gives thanks for a posterity she deserved never to have, rejects the subtler reading which makes her claim the promised conqueror already in her arms, and takes her rather to offer the child to God as the first-fruits of his race.

Henry thinks the brothers were twins, the pair recalling Esau and Jacob, the elder hated and the younger loved. On the names he warns that if Eve did think this son the promised seed she was wretchedly mistaken, as Samuel was when he said, Surely the Lord's anointed is before me: when children are born, who can foresee what they will prove, since he that was thought to be a man from the Lord became an enemy to the Lord, and the less we expect from creatures the more tolerable will disappointments be. Abel he takes for vanity, given by a mother so taken up with her first possession that another son was as nothing to her, and presses the name on the whole race, since every man at his best estate is vanity.

Clarke calls it extremely difficult to ascertain what Eve meant, and rejects the common view that she took Cain for the promised seed as too refined for that period; more likely she meant no more than to acknowledge that it was through God's peculiar blessing that she conceived. Unless she had been under divine inspiration, he adds, she could not have called her son Jehovah, and that she was not so inspired her mistake sufficiently proves. Wesley reads the name Cain as possession, spoken with joy and thankfulness and great expectation.

Ellicott alone presses the harder rendering, who is Jehovah, on the ground that the particle cannot mean one thing here and another in the first verse of the book; the objection that this implies too advanced a knowledge he calls unfounded, since we read backward and put our own ideas into the narrative, whereas these words were only the germ, the filament in the acorn which contains the oak. In Eve's mouth the title probably meant no more than the coming One. He looks ahead to what the chapter will show, the founding of a family godless and wanton which nevertheless far outstripped the sons of Seth in the arts of civilisation.

debates.question: What did Eve mean by the words rendered from the LORD?

positions.position: that she gives thanks for a posterity she had deserved never to have, offering the child to God as the first-fruits of his race
only that she conceived through God’s peculiar blessing; the messianic reading is too refined for that period
a man, even Jehovah — not a developed messianic idea, but the germ of one, meaning the coming One

themes: I have gotten a man from the LORD
whether Eve took her firstborn for the promised seed
Cain possession and Abel vanity

2.pericope_label: She bare his brother Abel; Abel was a keeper of sheep, Cain a tiller of the ground

schools.summary: Gill allows that the second birth may have followed the next year, though some have thought from the silence about a second conception that the two were born together, and passes on the Jewish opinion that a twin sister was born with Abel; on the name he notes that it means not mourning, as Josephus said, but vanity, either because Eve made no such account of this son as of her first, or because by a spirit of prophecy she foresaw his violent death. Calvin will not have the name spoken in contempt, which he calls perfectly absurd; rather Eve, having celebrated in her firstborn the joy that suddenly burst upon her, turned in her second to the recollection of the miseries of the human race, holding up a common mirror to admonish her whole progeny. He insists that both callings were in themselves holy and laudable, whence he infers that the brothers had been well instructed by their father, and notes that Cain's life was in appearance very well regulated.

Clarke thinks the wording settles the matter for twins, since where successive births are recorded Scripture usually mentions conceiving and bringing forth for each child, whereas here it is simply that she added to bring forth Abel his brother; he counts three primitive employments, Adam a gardener, Abel a shepherd, Cain a farmer, and calls them the most rational and the best calculated to prevent strife and an immoderate love of the world. Wesley finds an advantage in the pastoral calling, which most befriends contemplation and devotion, Moses and David having kept sheep and in their solitudes conversed with God.

Ellicott looks at the interval before Seth, which leaves a long period for the family to increase and for the characters of these two to develop, and sees in the one a rough strong nature that took the hard work as it found it, in the other a nature more refined and thoughtful. He dismisses Oppert's Assyrian etymology of the name, since the Hebrew means a thing unstable and not abiding, like a breath or vapour, and doubts that a mother named her child from a presentiment at all, the title more probably being given after his death. Keil hears in it that her joy was soon overcome by the discovery of the vanity of this earthly life, observes that the occupations are noticed on account of what follows, and adds that God himself had pointed out each to Adam, tillage in the employment assigned in Eden and the keeping of cattle in the clothing he gave.

debates.question: Why was the second son called Abel?

positions.position: from Eve’s lower account of him, or from a prophetic foresight of his violent death
as a monument of her sorrow, holding up a mirror of human vanity to her whole progeny
probably as a title given after his death, when his relatives called him the breath that had passed away

themes: she added to bear his brother Abel
whether Cain and Abel were twins
two callings both holy and laudable

3.pericope_label: In process of time Cain brought of the fruit of the ground an offering unto the LORD

schools.summary: Gill reports the view that at the end of days means the end of a week, on the seventh day, but objects that this proceeds on a hypothesis not sufficiently established, that a sabbath was already appointed to be kept religiously; he prefers Aben Ezra's reading, at the end of the year, which would fall after harvest when gratitude was in season, and adds that the Targum of Jonathan fixes the day to the fourteenth of Nisan, as though it were the passover, a feast instituted two thousand years later.

Henry has the brothers bring their offerings to Adam as the priest of the family, and thinks there was a divine appointment given to Adam for it, as a token of God's favour notwithstanding their apostasy, by which God would try Adam's faith and settle a correspondence again between heaven and earth. He draws four lessons: that the religious worship of God is no novel invention but the good old way, truth having got the start of error and piety of profaneness; that it is good for children to be trained up betimes in religious services; that we should honour God with what we have, according as he has prospered us; and that hypocrites may be found going as far as the best of God's people in the external services of religion, since Cain's offering is even mentioned first, as if he were the more forward of the two.

Clarke inclines to the sabbath, since divine worship was certainly instituted in that family, and describes the worship as very simple in its original institution and consisting of two parts, thanksgiving to God as the author of all the bounties of nature and piacular sacrifices to his justice and holiness, implying conviction of sinfulness, confession, and faith in the promised Deliverer; of Cain's own offering he notes that the word is the one explained in Leviticus as an offering of fine flour with oil and frankincense. Wesley leaves the season open and settles for some set time.

themes: at the end of days, whether of the week or of the year
a divine appointment of sacrifice given to Adam
hypocrites going as far as the best in outward service

4.pericope_label: Abel brought of the firstlings of his flock; the LORD had respect unto Abel and his offering

schools.summary: Gill takes the firstlings as a type of Christ, Jehovah's firstborn, the Lamb of God without spot or blemish, fitly signified by a lamb for his innocence, harmlessness and meekness, and denies that the matter of Cain's offering was the difficulty, putting it down rather to its being brought in a formal and hypocritical manner. Calvin notes the order Moses observes, since he does not say the oblation pleased God but begins with the person, signifying that God regards no works whose doer is not already accepted; man sees what is apparent, but God looks into the heart. He will not have the Hebrews' account that the sacrifice was consumed by celestial fire, since we ought not to invent miracles for which we have no testimony of Scripture, and thinks Cain judged rather from what followed. In him Calvin sees the likeness of every wicked man who wishes to be esteemed just, labouring at external works while presenting God with a mask.

Clarke reports Kennicott's reading, that Abel brought a gratitude offering like his brother's and besides it a victim from the first-born of his flock, by which alone he acknowledged himself a sinner, though he notes that Magee has criticised the distinction and thinks little is gained by the counter-criticism; on Cain's anger he observes that the displeasure which should have been turned against his own unhumbled heart was turned against an innocent brother. Wesley sets out three differences, in the persons, in the offerings, since Cain's was only a sacrifice of acknowledgment while Abel's was one of atonement, and greatest of all that Abel offered in faith; in the fallen countenance he finds not so much grief as malice and rage.

Jamieson, Fausset and Brown look at the verb of acceptance, which signifies to look at a thing with a keen earnest glance and has been rendered to kindle into a fire, so that the divine approval of Abel's offering was shown in its being consumed. Ellicott renders the Hebrew of the anger as it burned to Cain exceedingly, his heart being full of hot indignant feelings at the preference shown to a younger brother.

debates.question: How did Cain know that his brother's offering was preferred?

positions.position: by fire from heaven, the verb of acceptance itself meaning to kindle into a fire
not by any miracle, for which Scripture gives no testimony, but from the events that followed

themes: the LORD had respect unto Abel and to his offering
the person accepted before the work
Cain was very wroth, and his countenance fell

6.pericope_label: The LORD said unto Cain, Why art thou wroth? and why is thy countenance fallen?

schools.summary: Gill says the question was not asked in ignorance of Cain's wrath but to bring him to a conviction of the sins which had caused his sacrifice to be rejected, and so to repentance and amendment, and to show him that he had no cause to be displeased with God or with his brother, the fault lying in himself. Calvin takes the address as a citation to God's tribunal, that the wretched man might understand his rage could profit him nothing; and on the manner of the speaking he rejects the suggestion that Adam spoke as the prophet and interpreter of God, calling it constrained and even frigid. He understands what good men intend by such a fancy, namely to honour the external ministry of the word and to cut off the occasion Satan takes to insinuate illusions under colour of revelation, and grants that nothing is more useful than that pious minds be kept under the order of preaching; yet the word was delivered from the beginning by oracles, and they who think God spoke only through his ministers too violently restrict the words of Moses.

Henry makes it an instance of God's patience and condescending goodness that he should deal thus tenderly with so bad a man in so bad an affair, and sets the scene beside the father of the prodigal arguing with his elder son. From the form of the question he takes a lesson in self-examination, that God notices all our sinful passions, since there is not an angry look, an envious look, nor a fretful look that escapes his observing eye, and that most of our sinful heats would vanish before a strict enquiry into their cause: why am I wroth, is there a real cause, a just cause, a proportionable cause for it? He adds that Cain had no reason to be angry with God, who proceeded by the settled rules of a government suited to a state of probation, setting before men life and death and rendering to them according to their works.
Clarke calls the question a gracious warning and a preventive of the meditated crime.

themes: why is thy countenance fallen?
God reasoning with a murderer before the murder
whether the voice was God’s own or Adam’s

7.pericope_label: If thou doest well, shalt thou not be accepted? and if not, sin lieth at the door

schools.summary: Gill allows a general and a particular sense, either doing good works in a right manner, whence the saying that not nouns but adverbs make good works, or offering rightly, in the faith of the promised seed. Calvin surveys the older attempts and rejects most: the Greek translators, working before the vowel points, struck into an extraneous sense, while among those who keep the Hebrew some refer the word to Cain's countenance, some to the remission of sins, and some to honour. His own reading is that it means acceptance, opposed to rejection, and refers to the sacrifices, God being ready to receive them with outstretched hands if they ceased to be faulty; and he presses that the blame of the whole evil lay with Cain, who did what wicked men do when convicted, trying vainly to transfer the cause of the evil to others.

Clarke takes the noun in a sense he says he has traced through more than a hundred places of the Old Testament, a sin-offering, so that an animal proper for atonement is now couching at the door of Cain's fold; his fault had been to bring none when his brother brought one, and God graciously tells him his case is not yet desperate, since how many sinners perish, not because there is no Saviour able and willing, but because they will not use what is within their power. On the last clause he says expressly that the words are not spoken of sin, as many have understood, but of Abel's submission to Cain as his superior, to remove Cain's envy. Wesley keeps the shortest sense: sin only hinders his acceptance; and he draws out two readings of the first clause, either that Cain would have been accepted had he done well, since there is not a damned sinner in hell but, had he done well, had been a glorified saint in heaven, or that he might yet be accepted if he would repent, which shows how early the gospel was preached.

Ellicott calls this the most difficult verse of the chapter, capable of a satisfactory sense if we refuse to read the ideas of a later age into so ancient a narrative; literally it asks, if thou doest well, is there not lifting up, the promise being that instead of a downcast look Cain shall lift up his head and have peace beaming in his eyes from a quiet conscience. He gives two constructions of the second half and prefers the second, since though sin may be pictured crouching like a beast of prey at the door, sin is feminine while the verb and pronouns are masculine, an objection most Jewish interpreters override with what he calls a feeble explanation; on the second construction the desire and the rule belong to the brother. He fills in the circumstances of the jealousy and reads the remonstrance as evidence of a struggle in Cain's conscience, since Jehovah would not have reasoned thus kindly with a man altogether reprobate.

positions.position: a sin-offering, an animal proper for atonement couching at the door of the fold
sin itself, crouching like a beast of prey, though the grammar tells against making it the subject of what follows
sin as the one hindrance to acceptance

debates.question: Whose is the desire in the last clause?

positions.position: Abel’s, submitting to his elder brother; the words are not spoken of sin at all

themes: if thou doest well, is there not lifting up?
sin, or a sin-offering, lieth at the door
unto thee shall be his desire, and thou shalt rule over him

8.pericope_label: Cain rose up against Abel his brother, and slew him

schools.summary: Gill passes on the Jerusalem Targum's report of the brothers' talk, Cain arguing that there is no judgment and no Judge and no mercy in the world's creation or government, and Abel answering point by point. Calvin weighs two accounts of the talking: either Cain dissembled and spoke familiarly to keep up an appearance of fraternal concord until the opportunity came, whence the rule that hypocrites are most to be dreaded when they converse under the pretext of friendship, or, as he rather inclines to think, he broke out in open accusation against his brother.

Henry sets down the aggravations. It was his own brother, whom he ought to have loved, and a younger brother, whom he ought to have protected; a good brother, who had never provoked him in word or deed; he had fair warning and persisted; he covered the design with a show of friendship, as Joab kissed Abner and Absalom feasted Amnon; and in killing him he struck directly at God, since God's accepting Abel was the provocation pretended, and he hated Abel for the very reason that God loved him. The murder was the more inhuman because there were then so few men in the world. He traces the root as well: Adam's eating of forbidden fruit seemed but a little sin and opened the door to the greatest, and as Abel leads the van in the noble army of martyrs, so Cain stands in front of the ignoble army of persecutors.

Clarke notes that the Hebrew says only that Cain said to his brother, the best editions leaving a space with a mark referring to a note that something is wanting; the deficiency is supplied by the Samaritan text, the Syriac, the Vulgate, the Septuagint, the Targums and the Coptic, all reading, let us go out into the field, and since the words are lost from every known manuscript and yet stood in copies used before the Christian era, he thinks they may safely be counted part of the sacred text. He supposes the first murder was the fruit of a religious dispute, and remarks that millions have since been sacrificed to bigotry and intolerance, here having originated the many-headed monster of religious persecution. He marks what was new: this is Satan's first triumph, not merely a death but a violent one, not of an ordinary person but of the most holy man then living, and by a brother's hand. Wesley turns to the other side: the first who dies is a saint, and the first to the grave went to heaven.

Ellicott is more cautious about the addition: no Hebrew authority but the Jerusalem Targum supports it, though the versions carry great weight, the Hebrew manuscripts being all comparatively modern and representing only the Masoretic recension. He rules out our version's rendering, which would imply that Cain had triumphed for a time over his anger and resumed friendly intercourse, and concludes that either we accept the versions or must regard the passage as beyond our powers. He will not have the murder premeditated, since Cain did not know what a human death was, and offers Philippson's suggestion of the perpetual struggle between husbandmen holding fixed plots and shepherds whose flocks stray on tilled ground.

positions.position: yes — the friendly talk was a dissembling that covered the design until opportunity served
no — Cain did not yet know what a human death was; a quarrel over trespassing flocks turned to blows

themes: the words wanting in the Hebrew: let us go out into the field
the first murder as the fruit of a religious quarrel
the first that dies is a saint

9.pericope_label: Where is Abel thy brother? And he said, I know not: Am I my brother's keeper?

schools.summary: Gill supposes the question came when Cain next appeared to offer without his brother, asked not from ignorance but to bring him to conviction and confession, the mention of the relation being itself an aggravation. Calvin holds that those who suppose the father made the inquiry enervate the whole instruction, since God cited the murderer to his tribunal as if he had thundered from heaven; and though he may have been interrogated by the silent examinations of conscience, it was by a divine voice and not by the voice of a man. From this he draws his chief lesson, that as often as the secret compunctions of conscience invite us to reflect upon our sins we should remember that God himself is speaking with us, that interior sense being his peculiar judgement-seat. He notes the cavil exactly: Cain thinks to escape by pleading he had no express command to take care of his brother.

Henry sets it as a trial, since civil courts were not yet erected and God himself sits Judge; some think Cain was examined on the next sabbath, when the sons of God came to present themselves before the Lord and Abel was missing, whose place did not use to be empty, for the God of heaven takes notice who is present at and who is absent from public ordinances. He finds Cain covering a deliberate murder with a deliberate lie, so that in him the devil was both murderer and liar from the beginning; those are strangely blind who think it possible to conceal their sins from a God who sees all, and strangely hard who think it desirable to conceal them from a God who pardons only those that confess. He ends on the duty the retort denies: a charitable concern for our brethren as their keepers is strictly required and generally neglected.
Wesley gives the impudence plainly, that surely he is old enough to take care of himself, and adds the reflection some have heard in it upon providence, Art not thou his keeper?

Keil states the rule shortly: defiance grows with sin and punishment keeps pace with guilt, since Adam and Eve feared before God and acknowledged their sin while Cain boldly denies his. Ellicott reconstructs the state of mind, since Cain went away at first scarcely conscious of the greatness of his crime, having asserted his rights against a younger son's usurpation of his privileges, but could not quiet his conscience, and when Abel came not to the household and the question was asked, the voice of God repeated it in his own heart.

themes: I know not: am I my brother’s keeper?
conscience as the judgement-seat of God
a charitable concern for our brethren as their keepers

10.pericope_label: The voice of thy brother's blood crieth unto me from the ground: now art thou cursed

schools.summary: Gill takes the curse to mean that Cain is cut off from the benefit of the earth and from any settled dwelling in it. Calvin reads the sentence as a court scene brought to its end, since God no longer asks whether the thing was done but pronounces in a single word that Cain was the doer; advocates place their first defence in denying the fact and where it cannot be denied have recourse to qualifying circumstances, and Cain is driven from both. Three things he finds shown: that God is cognizant of men's deeds though none accuse them; that he holds the life of man too dear to let innocent blood be shed with impunity; and that he cares for the pious after death as well as before, since Abel was speechless when his throat was being cut, yet after death the voice of his blood was more vehement than any eloquence of an orator. On the ground he rejects the notion that cruelty is ascribed to the earth, as though it were a wild beast that had drunk the blood; rather clemency is imputed to it, there being more humanity in the earth than in the man.

Clarke supposes Cain had buried the body to prevent the murder from being known, which is what the opening of the ground implies, and mentions the opinion that the cry is that of Abel's widow and children, his occupation and sacrifices making it probable he was a father of a family. Wesley describes the figure: the words speak as if the blood were both witness and prosecutor, while the earth did as it were blush to see her face stained with such blood and opened her mouth to hide what she could not hinder; and on the choice of avenger he says God could have taken vengeance by a stroke from heaven but chose to continue him upon the earth and make even that his curse.

Keil quotes Delitzsch, that innocent blood has no voice discernible by human ears but has one that reaches God, murder being one of the sins that cry to heaven; he weighs two constructions of the preposition, either away from the earth, so that it afford him no quiet resting-place, or out of the earth, by its withdrawing its strength, and inclines to the second, rejecting as unsupported the notion that the soil became an accomplice by drinking the blood. Ellicott follows the thought forward: with the first shedding of human blood there sprang up the ominous conviction that the earth will grant no peace to the wretch who has stained her fair face with the life stream of man; but the blood of Jesus speaks better things than Abel's, the one voice crying for justice and retribution, the other for reconciliation and peace.

themes: the voice of thy brother’s blood crieth unto me from the ground
cursed from the earth, which hath opened her mouth
the blood of Jesus speaketh better things than that of Abel

12.pericope_label: A fugitive and a vagabond shalt thou be; my punishment is greater than I can bear

schools.summary: Gill notes that tillage was the business Cain had been brought up in. Calvin treats the first clause as expounding the curse just pronounced, since it says more clearly that the ground defrauds its cultivator of the fruit of his toil, and answers the objection that this was already laid on all men in Adam by saying that something of the blessing hitherto remaining was now further withdrawn from the murderer. On the wandering he sets aside the distinction some draw between the two Hebrew words and says the sense is that wherever Cain came he should be as robbers are, who have no quiet resting-place; he meets the objection that to be a stranger on the earth is rather the condition of the sons of God by observing that the faithful carry a sedate mind wherever necessity drives them, whereas even the first builder of a city was always restless in his own nest. On the cry he takes the words in their proper signification, that a greater punishment is imposed than Cain can bear, so that he complains of the severity of his judgment as devils do who feel themselves justly tormented and still charge God with cruelty.

Henry weighs both readings of the cry. If the words are those of despair they affront the mercy of God, since there is forgiveness with the God of pardons for the greatest sinners, though those forfeit it who despair of it; just now Cain made nothing of his sin and now he is in the other extreme, Satan driving his vassals from presumption to despair. But he judges the language rather that of indignation, complaining not of the greatness of the sin but of the extremity of the punishment. He follows the complaint into parts: Cain sees himself excluded from the favour of his God, expelled from the comforts of this life, and exposed to the ill-will of all mankind, so that like a man in debt he thinks every one he meets a bailiff; and he adds Lightfoot's suggestion that the last words are a wish, that any who find him may kill him.

Clarke prefers the margin, that the words may be rendered, Is my crime too great to be forgiven, since the noun signifies the crime rather than the punishment and the verb means to remit; they were uttered, he thinks, on the verge of black despair.
Keil observes the answer: though Cain expressed no penitence but only fear of punishment, God displayed his long-suffering and gave a promise.

debates.question: Is Cain's cry despair, indignation, or a question?

positions.position: indignation rather than despair — a complaint of the punishment, not of the sin
a question uttered on the verge of black despair: is my crime too great to be forgiven?

themes: when thou tillest the ground it shall not yield unto thee her strength
my punishment, or my iniquity, greater than I can bear
unpardoned guilt filling men with continual terrors

14.pericope_label: Every one that findeth me shall slay me; and the LORD set a mark upon Cain

schools.summary: Gill explains the banishment as exclusion not from the earth but from a quiet settlement in it, from society and converse with its inhabitants, and especially from the ground he had manured and the place where his parents dwelt. On the particle that opens the answer he reports the rendering as two words meaning not so, denying both Cain's fear and his wish to be killed by the first man he met, and prefers verily or surely, God's will being that Cain should not die at once but live a long miserable life, for a terror to others. Calvin allows that Cain reasons justly, since the hand of God alone preserves us amid so many dangers; yet he notes what the fear reveals, that since man is a social animal it is a portentous thing that the meeting of any man should be formidable to the murderer. He rejects the Jewish reading which breaks the sentence in two and refers the sevenfold punishment to Cain himself, and holds that God grants nothing to the murderer for his own sake but consults for posterity; the mark, he says, was set to strike terror into all, who might see in it as in a mirror the tremendous judgment of God against bloody men.

Clarke counts the parts of the punishment and finds Cain adding to them: God had named the cursed ground and the vagabond life, to which the man adds being hidden from God's face, the apprehension of being slain, and the terrors of a guilty conscience. On the mark he gathers from Shuckford the conjectures made and calls them frivolously curious: that Cain was made paralytic, from the Septuagint's groaning and trembling; that it was a letter of the divine name; that it was Abel's dog, which constantly accompanied him; and, from one rabbi wiser than all the rest, a long horn growing out of his forehead. With Shuckford he would translate that the Lord appointed to Cain a token, since to have marked him would have been the likeliest way to bring on him all the evils he dreaded. Wesley puts the reason for the sevenfold vengeance shortly: God having said vengeance is his, it had been a daring usurpation for any man to take the sword out of his hand; and he dismisses the question of the mark in a line, since God has not told us what it was and therefore the conjectures of men are vain.

Ellicott notes that most versions have not so, which requires only a slight change of the text, and explains the sentence given instead: the punishment was severe because the crime sprang from violent passions, but the life was not taken because the act was not premeditated, while anyone killing him would be a murderer indeed, so the vengeance would be sevenfold, that is complete. In this, he adds, is the germ of the law that set apart cities of refuge for the involuntary manslayer. On the mark he says the common rendering suggests an utterly false idea, since Cain was not branded in any way; the Hebrew says Jehovah appointed unto him a sign that no one finding him should slay him, probably some natural phenomenon whose regular recurrence would assure him of his security.

outliers.note: Collects the rabbinic conjectures about the mark — paralysis, a letter of the divine name, Abel's dog, a horn in the forehead — and calls the whole class of them frivolously curious.

themes: whosoever slayeth Cain, vengeance shall be taken on him sevenfold
a sign appointed, not a brand set
the germ of the cities of refuge

16.pericope_label: Cain went out from the presence of the LORD, and dwelt in the land of Nod

schools.summary: Gill offers two senses of the departure, either from the place where the Lord had been speaking with him or from where the divine Majesty usually resided at the east of Eden, Cain being now forbidden to appear among God's worshippers; and he notes a place near Tripoli in Syria, mentioned by Polybius and Strabo as the face of God, which may have been so named from a tradition that there God's presence was enjoyed after the expulsion from Eden. Calvin allows two accounts, either that Cain, having lived in the earth as in an abode belonging to God, now wanders like an exile beyond the limits of his protection, or that he had stood at the bar until condemned and, the speaking over, hastened elsewhere to escape the eyes of God; he thinks the region was named from its inhabitant, and infers from its lying east of Paradise that the garden must have been a limited place.

Henry reads the going out as a willing surrender of that part of the sentence: Cain renounced religion and was content to forego its privileges so that he might not be under its precepts, forsaking Adam's family and altar and never coming among good people again; hypocritical professors who have trifled with God are justly left to themselves, and hell itself is destruction from the presence of the Lord. He finds defiance in the choice of ground, since it was on the east of Eden that the cherubim stood with the flaming sword, and there Cain chose his lot as if to defy the terrors of the Lord.

Clarke reports that since the word is the same as that for a vagabond, some would render the clause as saying that Cain went out from the presence of the Lord, from the east of Eden, and dwelt a vagabond on the earth, so that the curse was thereby accomplished. Wesley takes the name as descriptive of the man rather than the ground, since the land he dwelt in was to him a land of shaking or trembling, because of the continual restlessness of his own spirit; those who depart from God cannot find rest anywhere else.

Keil says the situation cannot be determined, and that Nod denotes a land of flight and banishment set against Eden, the land of delight, where Jehovah walked with men; he is concerned rather with the wife, since the text assumes as self-evident that she went with him into exile and was a daughter of Adam, the marriage of brothers and sisters being inevitable among the children of the first men. Ellicott supposes Adam's family worshipped with their faces towards Paradise, so that Cain reckoned himself beyond the range of the vision of God, and records that Knobel supposed the land to be China, which he thinks too remote, while read without vowels the word becomes India; since none of Noah's descendants are described as travelling eastward, many regard the Mongol race as Cain's offspring.

themes: he went out from the presence of the LORD
the land of Nod, that is, of wandering
those who depart from God can find rest nowhere else

17.pericope_label: Cain knew his wife; and he builded a city, and called it after his son Enoch

schools.summary: Gill will not decide whether the wife was his sister or a niece by another son of Adam, this being about the hundred and thirtieth year, though at first Cain could marry none but a sister; he passes on two rival traditions, the Jewish one that Cain's own twin sister was not beautiful, so that he said he would kill his brother and take his wife, and the Arabic one that Adam would have had each brother marry the other's twin sister. Of Irad he notes that nothing further is recorded in sacred or profane history. Calvin infers from the silence that Cain had married before the murder, since it would have been worth recording that a sister could be found who would not shrink from a man defiled with a brother's blood, and calls it a prodigy that a man who imagined he had as many enemies as there were men should raise children instead of hiding in some remote solitude. The city he finds at first sight contrary to the sentence, and concludes that the man, oppressed by conscience, contrived a new kind of defence, the others living dispersed through the fields only because they were less afraid; yet pride was mixed with the fear, since he called the city after his son, when his memory could pass on only to be held in execration.

Clarke observes that the son's name signifies instructed or dedicated, especially in sacred things, and takes it for some proof of Cain's repentance that he dedicated this son to God, to minister in his father's stead in the office from which Cain was excluded. Wesley takes the building as a token of settled separation from the church of God, and says the names that follow are but just mentioned, as not valued in comparison with God's children.

Ellicott reasons from the promise that Eve's conception should be greatly multiplied, so that a numerous offspring had grown up before Seth, one of Adam's daughters apparently cleaving to her brother in spite of the sentence of banishment and following him as his wife. He gives the son's name two senses, to train and to dedicate, allied in old times because teaching generally took the form of initiation into sacred rites, so that the name purposed a trained and consecrated man and prepares us for the Cainites' rapid advance in the arts of civilisation. He reads the verb as an imperfect, that Cain began to build, there being not yet population enough for a city, and sees in the design a wise ruler rather than a religious man, whose purpose was much what the builders of Babel had.

themes: he builded a city, and called it after the name of his son
whether the name Enoch marks a change in Cain
the Cainite and the Sethite genealogies compared

19.pericope_label: Lamech took two wives; Jabal, Jubal and Tubal-cain and the beginnings of the arts

schools.summary: Gill calls Lamech the first we read of who introduced polygamy, against the institution by which one man and one woman were to become one flesh, and notes that the practice, begun in the race of wicked Cain, was afterwards followed by some among the people of God and connived at for the hardness of their hearts; he reports and rejects Jarchi's account that before the flood men kept one wife for children and another for pleasure, since both of Lamech's wives bore sons. Of the youngest son he notes that many identify him with Vulcan, the names and the trade agreeing. Calvin thinks it of little consequence whether Lamech was impelled by desire of enlarging his family or by mere lust, since either way he corrupted nature's laws with brutal contempt of God, and finds a providence in the choice of the first offender, the Lord willing that the corruption of marriage should proceed from the house of Cain, that polygamists might be ashamed of the example. On the arts he makes his chief point: with the evils that proceeded from that family some good had been blended, since the invention of arts serving the common use of life is a gift of God not to be despised, and it is wonderful that the race which fell most deeply should have excelled the rest of Adam's posterity in rare endowments. The sons of Cain, though deprived of the Spirit of regeneration, were endued with gifts of no despicable kind, and the liberal arts have descended to us from the heathen; God enriched them so that their impiety might have less excuse.

Henry draws two warnings from the polygamy: that those who desert God's ordinances lay themselves open to all manner of temptation, and that when a bad custom is begun by bad men, better men are sometimes drawn in unwarily, as Jacob and David were afterwards ensnared in this very sin. On the sons he counts three, a famous shepherd whom the shepherds of that age and after called father, a musician who first gave rules for that noble art, and a smith who improved the working of brass and iron for war and husbandry, matching them against the heathen gods as their Pan, their Apollo and their Vulcan; when Jabal had set them in a way to be rich, Jubal put them in a way to be merry. Yet he turns the account: common gifts are given to bad men while God chooses the foolish things of the world, and here was a father of shepherds and of musicians but not a father of the faithful, one to teach in brass and iron but none to teach the knowledge of the Lord.

Clarke says Lamech was the first who dared to reverse the order of God, and that from him polygamy has been retained and defended to the present day; he fills in the inventions, tent-making and the management of cattle in the first son, stringed and wind instruments in the second, both words being generic, and in the third the first smith on record, adding that some of these arts were useless while man was upright but became necessary after the fall, and that as the power to get wealth is from God so is the invention of useful arts. Wesley thinks the heathen Vulcan came from Tubal-cain, and confesses that why the sister is named he cannot say.

outliers.note: Defends music in particular, since though the harp ministers to pleasure rather than necessity it can serve the offices of religion, if free from vicious attractions and from the foolish delight that seduces men from better employments.

themes: the first transgression of the law of marriage
the father of such as dwell in tents, and of such as handle the harp
gifts of God scattered among a reprobate race

23.pericope_label: Lamech said unto his wives: I have slain a man to my wounding, and a young man to my hurt

schools.summary: Gill allows a penitent and a boastful sense, either that Lamech is confessing what he has done and reckoning how much sorer a punishment he deserves than Cain, or that he is quieting his wives with an argument that none may safely touch him. Calvin traces the obscurity to the abruptness of Moses, and clears away the Jewish fable that Lamech was a blind hunter whose boy misdirected his arrow so that it killed Cain in the woods, after which the master killed the boy. He prefers to resolve the past tense into a future and take it indefinitely, so that Lamech is boasting he has strength enough to strike down any enemy whatever, the repetition of man and young man being Hebrew amplification and not two persons. On the wives he observes that the soothing arts of wives often mitigate cruel men, whereas Lamech cast the venom of his cruelty into their bosom and broke out in threats of indiscriminate slaughter like a furious wild beast; and on the closing boast he says Lamech perverts the divine declaration and mocks its severity, taking greater licence to sin as though God had granted murderers a singular privilege, as Dionysius boasted that the gods favour the sacrilegious.

Henry marks how haughtily and imperiously he addresses his wives, and observes that it is no marvel that a man who had broken one law of marriage by taking two wives should break another which bound him to be kind and tender to them; those are not always the most careful to do their own duty who are highest in their demands of respect from others. He notes too that it is a common thing for fierce and bloody men to glory in their shame, caring not how many lives are sacrificed to their resentments so long as they are feared; and he says Lamech presumes impiously on God's protection, arguing that if God secured the life of Cain, who slew his brother upon no provocation, much more would he avenge one who killed only in a quarrel.

Clarke observes that the speech stands in hemistichs in the original, and since nothing of the kind occurs earlier thinks it very probably the oldest piece of poetry in the world; he supposes Lamech had slain a man in self-defence and that his wives feared the dead man's kindred would seek his life, and notes that the words may also be read interrogatively, Have I slain a man that I should be wounded. He declines to trouble his readers with the Jewish tale that Lamech killed Cain, though Jerome followed it, and leaves the passage among those he calls inscrutable. Wesley confesses at once that the passage is extremely obscure, since we know neither whom Lamech slew, nor on what occasion, nor what ground he had to be so confident of the divine protection.

debates.question: What is Lamech claiming to have done?

positions.position: to have killed a man in self-defence, and to be therefore safer than Cain was
nothing yet — the tense should be future, and he is boasting that he can strike down any enemy whatever
either confessing a murder or quieting his wives; the passage admits both
we cannot tell; the passage is extremely obscure

themes: the oldest piece of poetry in the world
if Cain shall be avenged sevenfold, truly Lamech seventy and sevenfold
a divine forbearance turned into a licence to sin

25.pericope_label: Adam knew his wife again, and she bare a son, and called his name Seth

schools.summary: Gill notes that the Targum puts a hundred and thirty years between the murder and this birth, but Ussher, more probably, places Seth in the same year. Calvin denies the inference that the first parents were left wholly childless, since it is incredible that while the benediction to increase and multiply was in its greatest force they should have been unfruitful through so many years; the house of Adam was already populous before Abel was slain, and Moses means only that the parents, horror-struck at the slaughter, abstained for a while from the conjugal bed. He says Eve means some peculiar seed, since others had been born before Abel's death, but the race being prone to evil nearly her whole family had corrupted itself, so that she reckoned herself bereaved, in Abel, not of one son only but of her whole offspring.

Henry notices that this is the first mention of Adam in the chapter, and that the murder of Abel and the apostasy of Cain were a very great grief to him and Eve, the more because their own wickedness now corrected them; when parents are grieved by their children's wickedness they should take occasion from it to lament that corruption of nature which was derived from them. He finds in the birth a rule of God's dealing, that when he takes away one comfort he gives another instead, and presses the point about the church, that the succession of confessors is the revival of the martyrs and as it were the resurrection of God's slain witnesses; those who slay God's servants hope thereby to wear out the saints of the Most High, but God can out of stones raise up children and make the blood of the martyrs the seed of the church. The name he gives as set, settled or placed, and draws the contrast that while Cain, the head of the apostasy, is made a wanderer, Seth, from whom the true church was to come, is fixed.

Clarke argues that Eve must have received some divine communication, since otherwise she could not have known that this son was appointed in Abel's place to continue the holy line by which the Messiah was to come, whence he concludes the line was determined from the beginning and not first fixed in Abraham's days; he traces it forward, since Seth's posterity alone continued after the flood, and observes that wherever there were two or more sons the chosen one was pointed out by especial providence. Wesley joins Henry in the account of the parents' grief and of the relief given them in another seed.

Ellicott renders the name appointed or substituted, the son being designated head of Adam's family, and makes the point of the succession, since instead of the third son simply taking the firstborn's place it is given to one specially marked out, probably by prophecy, as Solomon took the rights of primogeniture over Adonijah.

themes: God hath appointed me another seed instead of Abel
the succession of confessors as the resurrection of slain witnesses
Cain a wanderer, Seth one fixed

26.pericope_label: To Seth was born Enos: then began men to call upon the name of the LORD

schools.summary: Gill gives the usual interpretation of the son's name, a weak, frail, mortal and miserable man, given by a father who observed the sorrows of life and the growing corruptions of the age, but notes that it may also come from an Arabic word meaning to be sociable; on the clause that follows he is careful that it does not mean the first calling upon God, since Adam and Abel and all good men had called on his name before. Calvin finds a synecdoche in the verb, calling upon God standing for his whole worship and named from its principal part, since God prefers this service of piety and faith to all sacrifices, and warns that Satan contrives nothing with greater care than to adulterate the pure invocation of God. He takes the clause historically too, that the deluge of impiety was then so great that religion survived only with a few, until Seth begat a son like himself and had a rightly constituted family, whereupon the face of the Church began to appear; and he rejects as a foolish figment the construction which makes the verse date the beginning of idolatry, since Moses is not censuring superstitions here but commending the piety of one family.

Clarke reports that many eminent men would render the verb as began profanely, so that the words date idolatry's origin, most of the Jewish doctors being of that opinion, and sets out Maimonides, whose account runs that in the days of Enos the sons of Adam erred greatly, reasoning that since God had set the stars on high to govern the world it was meet that men should glorify what he honoured, whereupon they built temples to the stars and sacrificed to them, until the practice spread through all the world and the glorious and fearful name was forgotten out of the mouth of all living, save with a few, until Abraham was born. He draws the chapter's lesson from the other end: no uprightness of intention can atone for neglect of the positive commands of revelation, and he who brings a eucharistic offering while a sin-offering lies at the door copies Cain, whose envy begot hatred, and hatred malice, and malice murder. Wesley gives two senses of the beginning, either that the worshippers of God began to stir themselves up to do more in religion than of late, worshipping now not only in closets and families but in public assemblies, or that they began to be called by the name of the Lord and so to distinguish themselves, since Cain and those who had deserted religion called themselves the sons of men while those who adhered to God called themselves the sons of God.

Keil takes the name from a verb meaning to be weak, so that it expresses the knowledge of human frailty, the opposite of the pride displayed in the Cainite family, and observes that this feeling led to God and to the invocation which began under Enos. Ellicott doubts the derivation from mortality, for which there is no proof, and takes the word as the generic name for man, used so in Aramaic, where our Lord is styled the son of Enosh; he makes the beginning belong to the name rather than the worship, the notion of divinity being now first attached to Jehovah, which Eve had used without any such thought.

debates.question: What began in the days of Enos?

profanation — the verb may be read began profanely, and the verse dates the origin of star-worship
the attaching of divinity to the name Jehovah, which had carried no such sacredness before

whether the verse dates the beginning of true worship or of idolatry
the sons of God and the sons of men distinguished
